Issued at 440 AM EDT FRI JUL 24 2026

The main change to the grids for the first part of the extended 
forecast this morning was primarily to include some more terrain
distinctions into temperatures each night, though some uncertainty 
remains as to nocturnal sky cover. Strong 5h ridging to the west
supporting a glide path for shortwaves into eastern Kentucky to 
start the new work week appears to be a guiding principle of the 
extended weather pattern - one that would necessitate staying 
abreast of these minor features in order to time the best chances  
for significant storms - either organized or more of the typical 
summer-time, garden variety.

The previous long term discussion follows:

The long term period will be characterized by anomalously strong 
upper level ridging over the central/western CONUS, with well 
defined upper level troughing dominating the East Coast. This 
amplified pattern will place Kentucky in a region of northwest 
flow aloft for the entirety of the long term period, allowing for 
a series of shortwaves to pass through the area. Multiple rounds 
of showers and storms are expected over the course of the forecast
period, although the exact timing of this activity remains 
uncertain at this time, owing to increasing model spread in the 
progression of these smaller impulses (especially near the end of 
the period). 

On Saturday, southwesterly winds will continue to advect better 
moisture into our area, with dewpoints rising into the upper 60s 
for much of the forecast area by Saturday evening (and perhaps 
even the low 70s for our southwestern counties). Concurrently, a 
stalled boundary initially located over Tennessee will begin to 
lift north, finding itself near the KY/TN line by the evening 
hours, with weak WAA in the low levels in our southernmost 
counties. This, in addition to the potential for assisting 
shortwave perturbations, will lead to a chance for scattered 
showers and storms throughout the weekend, with the highest rain 
chances near the KY/TN line. Shear will remain fairly weak, so any
storms that do form will not bring a risk for organized severe 
weather, and will more so be typical pulse storms. However, the 
air mass in place ahead of this convection will be anomalously 
moist; LREF mean PW is generally in the range of 1.6-1.8 inches in
the southern portion of the forecast area, representing 75th to 
85th percentile PW values when compared to climatology. Given this
juicy environment, any storm that forms would be capable of 
producing efficient rainfall. Accordingly, the Weather Prediction 
Center has introduced a Marginal (Level 1/4) Risk for Excessive 
Rainfall for our counties closest to the TN line; this represents 
a chance for isolated flash flooding should a storm be able to 
capitalize on this moist environment, although the overall flash 
flood risk appears quite low at this point. There is some model 
disagreement regarding overnight activity going into Sunday 
morning, with an additional subtle wave represented in some 
models. Should this come to fruition, cloud cover would prevent 
any ridge/valley temperature split from developing overnight. 
However, if skies can clear out some, a modest ridge/valley 
temperature split could develop, with this outcome most likely in 
our northern counties that remain somewhat removed from the best 
rain chances. For now, have held off on the introduction of any 
ridge/valley split into the forecast grids due to cloud cover 
uncertainties; however, this may need to be adjusted as the timing
of shortwave energy becomes more certain. 

Rain chances decrease again on Sunday as the upper level ridge 
over the Great Plains amplifies and expands slightly east. 
Meanwhile, the trough to the east of the forecast area will 
continue to deepen. At the surface, winds will become more 
northwesterly, tapping into a very muggy upstream air mass that 
will drive further moisture advection. Temperatures will also 
continue to warm, with high temperatures in the upper 80s expected
across the forecast area, marking a return to hot and muggy 
weather, although nearby high pressure should keep rain chances 
fairly low during the day. Then, model guidance begins to diverge 
significantly by Sunday night, and especially next week.

Looking ahead, a period of active weather appears to be 
increasingly probable next week. Notably, the upper level pattern 
will be favorable for MCS type activity, with eastern Kentucky 
remaining on the eastern periphery of the highly amplified ridge 
over the Plains. In fact, the 12Z GFS shows a signal for a 
convective complex through the Commonwealth as early as overnight 
on Sunday, although this solution remains an outlier at this time.
